Angle Bisector Ratio

GeometryTrianglesAlgebra
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle and see where the line that splits the top corner in half lands on the far side.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Turn on Hint or Extra construction, then press Check the ratio.
Look for the math

A line that cuts a corner of a triangle exactly in half always lands on the far side in a very particular spot. Drag the corners and compare the two numbers below the picture: one stays equal to the other however you stretch the triangle.

The bisector and where it lands

An angle bisector splits an angle into two equal parts. Here the line from A meets the far side BC at D, and the two small arcs at A show the matching halves: angle BAD = angle DAC. The foot D slides along BC as you drag the corners, but it never leaves that side.

The ratio on the far side

The applet's page makes one exact claim: if AD bisects angle A, then the two side lengths beside A compare in the same way as the two pieces of BC:

AB / AC = DB / DC

This is the Angle Bisector Theorem. The logic test checks it on hundreds of triangles — acute, right, very obtuse and in both drawing orders — and the two numbers agree every time. When the triangle is isosceles at A, both ratios are 1 and D is the midpoint of BC.

Why it works: an isosceles triangle

Draw the line through C parallel to AD and let it meet the line AB at E. Turning on Extra construction shows it. Because the line is parallel, the angle at C equals the half angle CAD, which equals BAD, which also equals the angle at E; so triangle AEC is isosceles and AE = AC. The two similar triangles BEC and BAD then give BE / BA = BC / BD, which is the same statement as DB / DC = AB / AC.

The outside bisector and the converse

The outside bisector of angle A obeys the same rule, but it cuts the line BC outside the segment: the lengths from that point to B and to C still compare as AB to AC. The converse is just as neat — on a segment there is only one spot that divides it in a given ratio, so a point that splits BC as AB splits AC must be the foot of the bisector. Multiplying the three such ratios at A, B and C gives 1, which is Ceva's theorem: the three bisectors meet at one point.

Try making AB much longer than AC, then turn on Hint to see the equal steps that carry the ratio from one side to the other.
